comments.author: @dankasper3914
comments.text:
I didn't know this corner of the internet existed, but I guess I shouldn't be surprised. This is not about control or keeping you "trapped." You are not fenced in, and can still own a car, so can go wherever else you want to at any time. It helps you build community and making life more convenient, healthy, and happy. If you have ever lived in a place like this, you would know how great it is to be able to access most of what you need within a short walk, bike ride, or trip on public transportation. I used to live in the area immediately around the city center of Denver, and it was rare that I had to drive anywhere in the city. It was a great quality of life - I have never walked or rode my bike that much anywhere else I lived. It is more community-oriented and healthy. That's enough to make it desirable, but if you add in the emissions savings - including CO2, but even if you are a climate denier, you can't deny the benefits of having less smog and particulate matter in the air.

And if you are worried about surveillance, I have some bad news for you: There are license-plate reading cameras all over the country. There is nothing to indicate that it will be worse in Frisco than anywhere else. And the federal government (especially in the most recent administration) has the tech and AI companies so far up their asses that the companies are getting basically anything they want, civil liberties be damned.

And it's not a new concept at all! This is how cities USED to be designed before we became such a car-centric culture. See Jane Jacobs' The Death and Life of Great American Cities as an example. 

The average person spends about an hour a day driving just to and from work, and about 10% of people spend around 2 hours. Is that time well-spent? Is that money well-spent (especially considering gas prices)? I don't mind a short commute b/c it gives me time to myself, but I don't like being forced to do it. It is mostly a waste of time (our most precious resource) and money. Talk about being trapped! 

You are not forced to rent. There are homes for sale (albeit very expensive). And rents range from around $1,000 - $3,000. But you have to look beyond up-front cost into life cycle cost. The average American spends over $2,000 per year on gas (and that was before gas was $4.00/gallon). Add to that parking costs, car maintenance costs, healthcare costs of being more sedentary, wellness costs of living more isolated lives, and more. And you also save a lot of time. 

And guess what? This is still a free country and no one is making you move to these places. You want to live in the country? You can do that. You want to live in the suburbs? You can do that. You want to live somewhere very population dense? You can do that. You want to live here but keep your car so you can leave whenever you want.
